::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 11) you can:

1. **compute** a full-batch GNN's memory bill before training it, and quantify the neighborhood-explosion problem on a real graph;
2. **explain and contrast** neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE), Cluster-GCN, and GraphSAINT — what each samples, its bias/variance trade, and when each wins;
3. **derive** SGC from GCN (delete the nonlinearities, precompute the propagation) and state when the simplification is harmless — and how SIGN generalizes it;
4. **train** on a graph via mini-batching with a sampler you built yourself, and profile accuracy against time and memory honestly;
5. **sketch** a production serving story: precomputed embeddings versus on-demand inference, and what each costs.
:::

## The instruction that has been lying to you

Every GNN this course has trained contains one line so ordinary you stopped
seeing it: `out = net(data.x, data.edge_index)`. *The whole graph, as one
function argument.* Every node's features on the GPU at once, every edge's
message computed at once, every activation retained for backprop at once. On
the karate club that line is invisible; on Cora it is merely quaint; on
ogbn-arxiv —
169,343 nodes — our measured training peak was already **2,821 MB**, a third
of the course GPU, for a two-layer model of hidden width 128.

Now the numbers the industry actually lives with. The academic graph HGT
trained on: 179 million nodes. Pinterest's recommendation graph when PinSage
shipped: 3 *billion* nodes, 18 billion edges. Payment networks, social
graphs, the web itself: the graphs where graph ML earns salaries sit two
to five orders of magnitude past arxiv, and the one-line instruction
does not degrade gracefully across that gap — it simply stops, with a
CUDA out-of-memory error as its entire farewell. This week is about what replaces it, and the
answer will be satisfying for a specific reason: every escape route is an
idea you already own — SAGE's sampling bargain from Week 7, the cluster
structure of Week 2, the fixed propagation operator of Week 6 — reappearing
with a systems engineer's job description. Nothing genuinely new is invented this
week. Everything old is finally, honestly *priced*.

It is also the week this course's subject changes disciplines. Weeks 6–10
were applied mathematics: what functions can this architecture express,
what does this decomposition cost in parameters. This week's questions —
what fits in memory, what saturates a data pipeline, what can be
precomputed, what can be served at latency — are *systems* questions, and
the skills they exercise (back-of-envelope capacity math, profiling
before optimizing, constraint-first design) are the ones that
distinguish a graph-ML engineer from a graph-ML paper-reader in every
job interview this field conducts. The papers this week are read
differently too: their theorems are small, their Tables 3 are the
contribution, and the correct reading posture is the one you practiced
on ablation grids — find the matched comparison, find what was held
fixed, find what the headline hides.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** ogbn-arxiv's average degree is 13.8. Estimate:
how many *distinct* nodes, on average, live within three hops of a random
node — the set a 3-layer GNN must touch to compute one node's embedding? And
what fraction of the whole 169k-node graph is that?

::: {.predict-answer}
Measured over 200 random seeds: **22,663 nodes — 13% of the entire graph**
(1 hop: 18; 2 hops: 4,577). The naive estimate $13.8^3 \approx 2{,}600$ is
badly *low* because hubs dominate: one high-degree neighbor in the frontier
recruits its thousands. Three layers deep, "update one node" and "read an
eighth of the graph" are the same operation — that single measured fact is
the reason this lecture exists.
:::
:::

## The arithmetic of impossibility

Two separate resources run out, and it pays to audit them separately,
because different escapes fix different ones.

**The explosion (compute per node).** A node's $L$-layer computation tree —
Week 9's object, now billed — contains every walk of length $\le L$. On
arxiv, measured:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w11-explosion.html >}}

Why is the naive $\bar d^{\,L}$ estimate so wrong — 2,600 predicted,
22,663 measured? Because "average degree 13.8" is a statistical fiction
on a graph whose degrees follow the heavy-tailed shape Week 2 taught you
to expect: arxiv's median degree is far below its mean, while its top
nodes have thousands of neighbors, and a breadth-first frontier is
*biased toward hubs* — a random node probably isn't a hub, but a random
node's *neighbor* disproportionately is (the friendship-paradox
mechanic, now billing you for GPU memory). Two hops from almost
anywhere, the frontier has found a hub; three hops from anywhere, it has
found most of the graph's dense core. This is also why the explosion is
not an arxiv quirk but a law of the graphs that matter: social,
citation, purchase, and web graphs all carry the same tail, so
"three-layer receptive field ≈ a constant fraction of everything" is the
default planning assumption, not the worst case.

Run the arithmetic yourself at other budgets — and note carefully what the
fanout cap changes. Not the *average* so much as the *worst case*: an
uncapped batch that happens to touch one hub loads that hub's entire crowd,
so batch cost is decided by the graph's whims; capped at fanout $f$, the
cost is $\sum_k f^k$ *no matter what the graph does*. Predictable cost is
what schedulers, GPUs, and on-call engineers are made of:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w11-explosion.html >}}

**The residency (memory for the whole graph).** Full-batch training must
hold the graph's entire working set in GPU memory at once, and the audit
is worth doing line by line, because each line is a different villain and
a different escape targets each. Line one, the feature matrix: $N \times
d \times 4$ bytes in float32 — arxiv at $d{=}128$ is $169{,}343 \times
128 \times 4 \approx 83$ MB. Innocent. Line two, activations: every layer's
output must be *retained* until backprop consumes it, so a 2-layer model
holds two more 83 MB tensors plus the logits. Still innocent — under
300 MB so far, nowhere near our measured 2,821. Line three is the
culprit: **messages are per-edge, not per-node.** Before aggregation, an
implementation materializes one $d$-vector per directed edge — arxiv's
2.33 million directed edges at width 128 are $2.33\mathrm{M} \times 128
\times 4 \approx 1.2$ GB — and autograd retains what it must of that for
the backward pass, per layer. Suddenly 2,821 MB is not mysterious; it is
edge count doing what edge count does. (Fused scatter kernels avoid full
materialization; the measured number is what the standard PyG path costs,
which is what you will actually pay.) Line four, the bookkeeping tax:
gradients double every retained tensor's bill, and Adam's two moment
buffers triple every *parameter's* — negligible here (our model has ~38k
parameters), decisive for the 4.75M-parameter R-GCN layers of Week 10.

Before the escapes, dispose of the tempting non-answer: *just buy a
bigger GPU.* The arithmetic is unkind to it. Graphs of interest grow with
the businesses that own them — users, transactions, content, all
compounding — while accelerator memory grows on hardware-generation
timescales, and the bill scales with $E$, which for social and
transaction graphs grows *faster* than $N$. A strategy that needs
next year's card to train this year's graph is not a strategy; and even
where an 80 GB datacenter card postpones the wall, it converts a
$300-of-electricity training job into a five-figure hardware
dependency for what our table will show is often three accuracy points.
Scaling by hardware is how you buy time; scaling by algorithm is how
you stop needing to.

Do the same audit one benchmark up and the story ends. ogbn-products: 2.4
million nodes, 124 million edges. The feature line alone is 1.2 GB; the
edge-message line, at the same width, is $124\mathrm{M} \times 128 \times
4 \approx 63$ GB *before* retention. No consumer card, no datacenter
card, no near-future card: the scaling of the *bill* is linear in $E$,
and $E$ is the quantity the interesting graphs are made of. The audit's
punchline: full-batch memory scales with the graph, and the graph is the
one thing you cannot shrink. Except that shrinking the graph *per step*
is exactly what all three escapes do — sampling shrinks the tree,
partitioning shrinks the territory, precomputation removes the graph from
training altogether. Everything after this paragraph is those three
sentences, priced.

## Escape one: sample the neighborhood (and pay in time)

[Week 7](07-gnn-design.qmd) introduced GraphSAGE's fanout sampling as a
receptive-field curiosity. Reread it as a systems contract: *per batch,
load the targets, then at most $f$ neighbors per node per hop* — a
computation tree pruned to $O(f^L)$, which at $f{=}10$, $L{=}2$ means at
most 111 nodes per target instead of 4,577. Memory becomes a function of
batch size, not graph size. That is the entire idea; everything else is
implementation, and the implementation is where the week's most honest
lesson lives.

We built the sampler from scratch, and the construction deserves prose
because Lab 11 will make you build the same one and because every
production sampler is this algorithm with better engineering. Store the
graph as CSR: one long array of destination nodes sorted by source
(`dst_sorted`), one pointer array (`ptr`) so node $v$'s neighbors are the
slice `dst_sorted[ptr[v]:ptr[v+1]]` — Week 1's adjacency-list storage,
now load-bearing, because uniform sampling from a slice is O(fanout)
with no scan. One *block* of sampling then does: for each of the batch's
target nodes, draw $\le f$ neighbors from its slice; collect all drawn
edges as (source, batch-position) pairs; take the *union* of targets and
drawn sources; and — the fiddly step everyone gets wrong once — remap
every global node ID into a dense local index for this batch, because
the GPU tensors you are about to build have no idea 169,343 nodes exist.
Stack two blocks for a 2-layer model: the second block samples neighbors
*of the first block's union*, so the batch's working set is targets +
their sampled neighbors + those neighbors' sampled neighbors. Concretely,
at batch 1,024 and fanout 10: the bound says up to $1{,}024 \times 111
\approx 114$k node-slots, but the *union* is far smaller — overlapping
neighborhoods deduplicate, and hubs that appear in many trees are loaded
once — the explosion working *for* you at batch scale, for the same
reason it worked against you at graph scale. Training arxiv with this
hand-rolled loop:

test accuracy **0.605**, training peak **64 MB** — a working set
forty-four times smaller than full-batch's — and **12.2 seconds per
epoch**, against full-batch's 0.10.

Read that trade three times, because it is the one production always
rediscovers. Sampling bought a 44× memory reduction and paid for it with a
**122× slower epoch** — and the slowdown is not the GNN, which does *less*
math than before; it is the *sampler*: pure-Python neighbor selection,
tensor gathers, index remapping, all on CPU while the GPU idles. The
canonical cure is not "make the sampler fast" alone but *overlap*: a
producer-consumer pipeline in which CPU workers sample and assemble
batch $k{+}1$ while the GPU trains on batch $k$, so the sampler's cost
hides behind compute it was previously blocking. Every serious GNN
framework ships this (prefetching loaders, pinned-memory transfers,
multi-worker sampling); every serious deployment tunes it; and the
diagnostic is one line of profiler output — GPU utilization. Ours, with
the naive loop, sat near 5%. A tuned pipeline's sits near 90, on the
identical model, which is why "GNN training speed" discussions that
never mention the data pipeline are not serious. Scaling
GNNs is a data-pipeline engineering problem wearing a machine-learning
costume. The real systems — PyG's C++/`pyg-lib` samplers, DGL's, the
in-house ones at every large deployment — exist precisely to make this
loop fast: parallel workers, pinned memory, sampling as compiled code. The
algorithmic content is the fanout cap; the engineering content is the
other 121×.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w11-sampler.html >}}

What does 13%-in-three-hops mean for batch design, concretely? That
mini-batches over graphs are not the independent draws they are in
vision: two target nodes three hops apart *share* most of their
computation trees, so a batch's working set grows sublinearly in batch
size (our measured unions confirmed it), gradients within a batch are
correlated through shared ancestors, and the effective "examples per
epoch" is murkier than the loader's progress bar implies. None of this
breaks training — SGD is forgiving — but all of it warps the
intuitions imported from i.i.d. deep learning: batch-size scaling
laws, learning-rate heuristics, and "more data per step is better"
each need re-deriving on graphs, and mostly haven't been. When your
loss curves on sampled graph training look stranger than your vision
experience says they should, this paragraph is why.

Statistically, neighbor sampling is the gentle option: the aggregated mean
over a sampled neighborhood is an unbiased estimate of the full mean
([Week 7's](07-gnn-design.qmd) widget showed you its spread), so the
gradient is noisy but honest, and accuracy typically lands close to
full-batch — our 0.605 vs 0.665 gap is mostly the shorter training budget,
not the sampling. Three practice notes complete the contract. Fanouts are
chosen asymmetrically — larger at the layer nearest the targets (where
each sample matters most), smaller further out; the GraphSAGE paper's
25/10 remains a sane default, our 10/10 a budget one, and the right
answer is an ablation, not folklore. Uniform sampling is only the
simplest citizen of a family: degree-proportional sampling reduces
variance when hubs carry signal, and PinSage's personalized-PageRank
top-$T$ selection replaces sampling with a deterministic importance
ranking — "which neighbors matter" answered by Week 2's surfer rather
than by a coin; every choice here is a bias/variance dial you now have
the vocabulary to reason about rather than copy. And *evaluation* should not sample:
at test time you can afford full neighborhoods computed layer-by-layer
over all nodes (our harness does exactly this), because inference has no
optimizer variance to hide behind — a sampled prediction is a
different prediction every run, which is an incident report waiting for
a deploy.

<details>
<summary>PinSage: the story where this became an industry — one drawer</summary>
In 2018 Pinterest had the bipartite graph of Week 1 at a scale no one had
trained on: 3 billion pins and boards, 18 billion edges, and a business
need — recommend visually-and-topologically related pins. PinSage is
GraphSAGE with every slot re-engineered for that reality: neighborhoods
are not uniform samples but the top-$T$ nodes by personalized-PageRank
visit counts (Week 2's random surfer, hired as an importance sampler);
"aggregation" weights neighbors by those visit counts; training runs on
MapReduce with a producer-consumer pipeline so CPUs sample while GPUs
compute (the 122× problem, solved by overlap); and serving — the part
nobody's paper section reads but every engineer should — precomputes all
3 billion embeddings offline and ships them to a nearest-neighbor index.
The reported outcome was a large lift in user engagement, and the deeper
legacy was sociological: PinSage is the paper that turned "GNNs" from a
benchmark subject into a hiring category. Its every design decision is a
Week-2-or-7 idea multiplied by a systems constraint, which is the truest
one-line summary of this lecture.
</details>

## Escape two: cut the graph into pieces

Partition the nodes into clusters, keep only within-cluster edges, and
train on one cluster at a time: each step is *full-batch on a small graph*
— no sampler in the inner loop, plain GCN code unchanged from Week 6,
memory bounded by the largest cluster. That is Cluster-GCN, and its
engineering personality is the opposite of sampling's: where sampling
moved complexity into the data pipeline, partitioning moves it into a
one-time preprocessing job and keeps the training loop stupid. That
stupidity is worth money — sequential reads of one cluster's tensors
instead of random gathers across the whole graph, trivially
data-parallel across machines (a cluster per worker), and our measured
0.51 s/epoch (forty small full-batch steps) against the sampler's 12.2
says the inner loop won the time column by 24× while also winning the
memory column outright at 31 MB.

At the far end of this philosophy sits distributed training: partition
the graph across *machines*, one worker per shard, gradients averaged —
Cluster-GCN's logic promoted from memory management to cluster
architecture, with partition quality now deciding network traffic
(cross-shard neighbor fetches) instead of merely bias. The largest
published GNN systems all live here, and their engineering papers read
as love letters to good partitions.

The catch is printed in the construction: **between-cluster edges do not
exist during training.** The model literally never sees them; the
estimate is *biased*, unlike sampling's noisy-but-honest one — no amount
of extra epochs converges to the full-graph answer, because the
optimizer is faithfully minimizing the wrong objective. The repair has
two parts. Cut where the graph is thinnest: METIS-family partitioners
(coarsen the graph level by level, cut the small coarse graph well,
project the cut back up, refine) routinely keep the large majority of a
community-structured graph's edges inside clusters — Week 2's insight
that real graphs *have* communities, converted into a memory tool. And
Cluster-GCN's own second trick: per batch, stitch a random *group* of
several clusters together and train on their union, so edges between
grouped clusters come back stochastically — bias traded back toward
variance, at a memory price you control by group size.

Why does random partitioning keep so few edges, exactly? Do the
one-line calculation, because it is a lovely instance of thinking in
probabilities: a uniformly random 40-way partition puts an edge's two
endpoints in the same part with probability $1/40 = 2.5\%$ — the
measured retention is not an empirical accident but the formula itself,
landing on the nose. (And it hands you the METIS sales pitch for free:
any partitioner that beats $1/k$ is extracting real community
structure, and on graphs like arxiv good partitioners retain the large
majority of edges — the distance between $2.5\%$ and that majority is
exactly what Week 2's modularity was measuring.)

We ran the deliberately crude version — that uniformly **random**
partition into 40 parts, the worst possible cut — and it kept, as
predicted, only **2.5% of the edges**. Predict the accuracy before reading on; everyone predicts
catastrophe. Measured: **0.628**, at **31 MB** and half a second per
epoch. Two lessons hide in that number. First, arxiv's labels lean heavily
on node *features* (they are averaged text embeddings of each paper's
title and abstract), so even a
2.5%-of-edges graph plus features carries most of the signal — an echo of
Week 10's "measure what the graph is worth before paying for it." Second,
that is precisely why real deployments still bother with METIS: on tasks
where structure carries more of the load, the between-cluster bias is the
whole game, and 2.5% would be the catastrophe everyone predicted. A biased
method's report card is only as good as the task it was graded on.

**GraphSAINT** completes the family and fixes the bias on paper: sample a
small subgraph per step, train full-batch *within* it, and multiply each
node's loss term and each edge's message by inverse inclusion
probabilities so the mini-batch loss is provably unbiased for the
full-graph loss. The sampler is a design slot with three stock options —
uniform nodes (simple, misses structure), uniform edges (biases toward
hubs in a controllable way), or short random walks from random roots
(the practical winner: walk-visited subgraphs are connected and
community-shaped, Week 2's surfer once again doing the heavy lifting) —
and the inclusion probabilities are estimated once, empirically, before
training. It is the estimator-theory answer to the whole section: keep
partitioning's simple inner loop, buy back sampling's honesty with
importance weights — the same reweight-by-sampling-probability move this
course first met in Week 3's negative sampling and Week 4's
self-adversarial weighting, resurfacing as a systems tool. The family
portrait, then, in one taxonomy you should be able to reproduce cold:
*node-wise sampling* prunes each target's tree (unbiased aggregation,
variance in the gradient, sampler in the hot loop); *subgraph methods*
train on small graphs (Cluster-GCN: biased but simple and fast;
GraphSAINT: unbiased via reweighting); *decoupling* changes the question
(next section). Every scalable-GNN paper you will ever skim is a point
in this three-cornered space.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w11-methods.html >}}

## Escape three: stop propagating at training time entirely

The most radical option comes from staring at [Week 6's](06-gcn.qmd) GCN
until it confesses. Two layers:
$\mathrm{softmax}\big(\hat A\,\sigma(\hat A X W_0)\,W_1\big)$. Now delete
the nonlinearity $\sigma$ — the one piece with no obvious job on a
homophilous task — and the parentheses collapse:

$$\hat A\,(\hat A X W_0)\,W_1 \;=\; \hat A^2 X\,(W_0 W_1) \;=\; (\hat A^2 X)\,W.$$

Everything graph-shaped — $\hat A^2 X$ — is a **fixed matrix**, computable
once, offline, on a CPU, with sparse matrix products, before training
begins. Look at what the collapse did to each of this week's two
villains. The explosion: gone — sparse matrix–matrix products stream
over edges without ever materializing anyone's computation tree, and
the precompute's cost is a clean $O(K \cdot E \cdot d)$, paid once. The
residency: gone from training — the optimizer holds the *train split's*
rows of a feature table and a $d \times C$ weight matrix, and could not
name the graph's edge count if interrogated. What remains to train is a
logistic regression on precomputed features. That is SGC, and the deletion is not an approximation trick so
much as a scientific question aimed at every deep GNN: *was the depth doing
nonlinear computation, or just propagation?* Measured on arxiv: precompute
3.9 s, then **1.5 milliseconds per epoch**, test **0.638** — beating our
sampled SAGE, within three points of full-batch, trainable on a laptop with
the GPU reserved for the 171 MB of the training split. On homophilous
benchmarks, the answer to the question is mostly "just propagation," a
result that should permanently raise your bar for what "deep" must
demonstrate. (When does the deletion hurt? Exactly where the lecture arc
predicts: heterophily, tasks needing nonlinear feature interactions along
paths, and everything Week 9 placed above the ceiling — SGC is below even
GCN there.)

Pause on what kind of scientific object SGC is, because its 2019 arrival
was one of the field's great cold showers and the shape of the argument
travels. Dozens of increasingly ornate GNNs had reported gains over GCN;
SGC deleted GCN's only nonlinearity, reduced training to a logistic
regression, matched the benchmarks, and thereby reclassified several
years of "architectural progress" as, in large part, propagation plus
tuning. It is the ablation discipline of Week 7 executed at field scale —
the null model that every proposed complexity must beat *before* its
story is believed — and its descendants (linear models with better
diffusion, label propagation hybrids) still sit embarrassingly high on
homophilous leaderboards. When you meet a new architecture, the SGC
question — *what survives if I delete the learning between hops?* — is
the fastest honest test you can run.

SIGN generalizes the move constructively: precompute *several* operators'
diffusions — $\hat A X$, $\hat A^2 X$, a PPR-weighted diffusion, a
triangle-based one — concatenate them per node, and let an MLP mix the
columns. Each operator is one hand-designed "view" of the neighborhood
(the inception-module idea, transplanted); everything graph-shaped
remains offline; training and serving stay MLP-simple; and the accuracy
gap to trained message passing narrows further at a fraction of the
cost. A small zoo of Week 2-style graph features, computed once, feeding
an ordinary neural network: the wheel of this course turning full
circle, with the graph demoted — or promoted — to a feature factory.

How do you choose $K$? The widget above is the intuition pump — at $K=0$
the three planted errors sit unrepaired, by $K=2$ averaging has fixed two
of them, by $K=8$ everything is washing toward Week 9's dominant
direction — and Week 9 also gave you the quantitative handle: the
non-dominant signal decays like $|\lambda_2|^K$, so the sweet spot is
where enough smoothing has happened to denoise and not so much that the
classes blur, a number the graph's spectrum sets and validation finds.
In practice $K \in \{2, 3\}$ wins almost everywhere homophily reigns —
the same "2–3 layers" folklore that oversmoothing and the explosion
independently enforce on trained GNNs, now arriving from a third
direction. Three unrelated walls, all pointing at the same shallow
architecture: when a design constant is overdetermined like that, it
stops being folklore and starts being a fact about graphs.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w11-sgc.html >}}

## The table that decides deployments

All four contenders, one data set, one budget discipline, training-peak
memory measured honestly (inference excluded — a lesson our own harness
had to be taught during this experiment):

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w11-table.html >}}

{{< include ../assets/d3/w11-table.html >}}

The reading protocol for such tables — this week's method in miniature:
identify which column is your *binding constraint* (an 8 GB card: memory;
a nightly retrain SLA: epoch time × epochs; a leaderboard: accuracy), read
that column's best row, then check what its *other* columns cost you. No
row wins every column, on our table or any honest one. Practice on ours:
memory-bound → Cluster-GCN's 31 MB, paying 3.7 accuracy points and a
bias you must re-examine per task; retrain-often → SGC's milliseconds,
paying the expressiveness ceiling and 2.7 points; accuracy-bound and it
fits → full-batch, paying everything else. And the stress-test button is
the real exam: at products scale, memory columns that grow with the
graph turn red, columns that grow with the batch stay green, and the
architecture debate of Weeks 6–10 is suddenly subordinate to a systems
property none of those weeks mentioned.

Be equally clear about what the table *cannot* say, because tables like
it get quoted past their warranty. It is one dataset (feature-heavy,
homophilous), one budget discipline (small, matched), one
implementation quality per row (our Python sampler is deliberately
naive; a compiled one shifts its time column by an order of magnitude
without touching the others). The *shape* transfers — which columns
scale with what — but the *numbers* are arxiv's, and quoting "sampling
costs 6 accuracy points" or "partitioning is fine with random cuts" as
laws would be exactly the benchmark-folklore this course keeps
inoculating you against. Rerun the bake-off on your task; it costs an
afternoon and settles everything the table only gestures at.

## After training: the serving decision

A trained model is not a product; a system that answers queries is. Two
canonical designs, and the trade is staleness against latency:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w11-products.html >}}

**Precompute** (PinSage's choice): run inference offline over all nodes —
itself a scaling job, but an embarrassingly batchable one — store the
embeddings in a vector index, serve by lookup plus approximate
nearest-neighbor search. Serving is microseconds and GPU-free; the price
is *staleness*: a node's embedding reflects the graph as of the last
batch job, so the new user, the just-posted item, the fraud ring
assembled this afternoon are invisible until the next refresh. Size the
consequence with PinSage's own arithmetic: 3 billion nodes at $d{=}256$
float32 is roughly **3 TB of embeddings** — a storage system, a refresh
pipeline, and an ANN index are now part of your "model," and the nightly
batch job that recomputes them is a bigger compute line-item than
training ever was. Whether staleness is tolerable is a *product*
question, not an ML one: a pin recommendation an hour stale costs
nothing; a credit decision an hour stale is the incident. Note the irony
with relish: after three weeks of encoder sophistication, production's
favorite serving strategy is… a lookup table — Week 10's loser, rehired
at serve time, because the two settings weight freshness and cost
oppositely.

**On-demand**: sample the neighborhood at request time, run the forward
pass, return a fresh embedding. Always current — and every request pays
the sampler (the 122× lesson, now on the latency budget) plus a GPU in the
serving path. Budget it honestly for a fraud check: fanout 10 at two hops
is ≤111 nodes whose features must be *fetched* — from a feature store,
not a local tensor, so ~a millisecond per batched lookup if the store is
good and the batch is one — then a small forward pass, a few
milliseconds more; a well-built path answers in ~10 ms, a naive one
(sequential fetches, cold cache, Python sampler) in seconds, and the
difference between those two numbers is somebody's entire job. Fraud
detection often has no choice about paying it: the whole point is the
edge created *seconds* ago, and the graph's freshest region is exactly
where the money is.

Notice who has entered the room. The serving decision involves a feature
store's latency SLA, a batch scheduler's refresh cadence, a vector
index's recall/latency curve, an on-call rotation's tolerance for a GPU
in the request path — infrastructure owned by data-platform and serving
teams, not by whoever tuned the model. Mature graph-ML organizations are
built around exactly this seam: modelers own the accuracy column,
platform owns the time and memory columns, and the weekly argument
between them is conducted in precisely the units of our table. Learning
to speak both dialects — this lecture's actual syllabus — is worth more
on the market than any architecture in Weeks 6–10.

Real systems hybridize: precompute for the bulk, on-demand for hot or new
nodes, periodic refresh in between — and the SGC/SIGN route deserves a
special mention here, because "features precomputed offline, model is an
MLP" is not just a training trick; it is the *serving architecture* many
production stacks quietly prefer, GNN or not. A close cousin has become
standard enough to name: **distill the GNN into an MLP** — train the
graph model offline, then train a plain MLP on node features to imitate
the GNN's outputs, and *serve only the MLP*. On homophilous data the
student recovers most of the teacher's accuracy while serving with no
graph access at all — no sampler, no neighbor fetches, no staleness
pipeline — which converts the entire scaling problem of this lecture
into an offline concern. When a team tells you they "run GNNs in
production," a good fraction of the time this is what is actually
running.

Two more scaling tools fill out the practitioner's shelf, each one
sentence of idea. **Historical embeddings** (the GNNAutoScale line):
train on mini-batches, but where a batch's computation tree wants an
out-of-batch neighbor, substitute that neighbor's *cached activation
from the last time it was computed* — slightly stale inputs in exchange
for never expanding the tree; memory becomes strictly batch-bounded,
and the staleness provably shrinks as training converges. And
**distributed partitioned training**: at the true high end (products and
beyond), the graph is partitioned across machines and both data and
gradients flow between workers — Cluster-GCN's philosophy promoted to
cluster-of-machines, with the partition quality now deciding *network
traffic* rather than just bias. You will not implement either in this
course; you should recognize both on sight in systems papers and job
descriptions.

One honesty note on economics before the method section, because this
course promised you the truth about the field. The infrastructure this
lecture describes — samplers, feature stores, embedding pipelines, ANN
indexes, refresh jobs — is a real engineering investment, and the
question every team should ask before making it is Week 10's question at
system scale: *what is the graph worth on this task, measured?* A
well-tuned gradient-boosted model on hand-built features, with no graph
infrastructure at all, remains the deployed baseline in much of
industry, and it wins often enough that "we should use a GNN" is a
hypothesis, not a plan. The teams that succeed run the probe first —
exactly the features-only baseline this course has made you run every
single week — and buy the infrastructure when, and only when, the gap
pays for it.

## The method: capacity-plan before you train

The week's transferable procedure — run it before writing any model code,
the way this lecture ran it on arxiv:

**Bill the residency.** $N \times d \times 4$ bytes per activation layer;
edge-message terms $E \times d \times 4$ where the implementation
materializes them; ×2 for backprop retention; ×3 on parameters for Adam.
Compare to the device. If it fits with headroom, stop — full-batch is the
best-accuracy, least-code option, and our table says so. This
anti-recommendation deserves italics because cargo-culted scale
machinery is this subfield's most popular self-inflicted wound: the
median graph a working team actually touches — a company's citation-like
corpus, a mid-size social network, every dataset in this course —
*fits*, and the team that spends a quarter building samplers for it has
purchased variance, pipeline bugs, and 122× slowdowns to solve a
problem the audit would have dismissed in a minute. Scaling machinery
you don't need is complexity you paid for anyway.

**Probe the explosion.** Sample 100 nodes, count $L$-hop neighborhoods
(ten lines; Lab 11's exercise 1). This number, against your batch-size
plans, chooses between "sampling is optional" and "sampling is the
design" — and while you are there, look at the degree distribution's
tail, because it also predicts *which* sampler: heavy hubs argue for
importance-weighted or PPR-style selection over uniform draws, and a
near-regular graph (rare, but real in meshes and grids) makes uniform
sampling nearly free of variance and the whole decision easier.

**Pick the escape by the constraint that binds.** Memory-bound with
structure-heavy signal → sampling (honest gradients, pay in pipeline
engineering). Memory-bound, need dead-simple inner loops at massive scale
→ partition (accept bias, buy a good partitioner). Homophilous task,
retrain often, serve cheap → SGC/SIGN (question whether you needed
training-time propagation at all). Then run the small-scale bake-off —
our table took one GPU-hour to produce, and it settles arguments that
meetings cannot.

**Design serving on day one.** Ask "who consumes the embedding, how fresh,
at what latency" before training, because the answer (precompute vs
on-demand) decides the model you should train — a model too slow to serve
is a benchmark entry, not a system.

Watch the whole procedure run once on a fictional-but-typical brief: *10M
users, 200M follow edges, predict churn weekly, one 24 GB GPU, features
are 256-d.* Bill the residency: features $10^7 \times 256 \times 4
\approx 10$ GB; one retained activation layer, another 10; edge messages
$2 \times 10^8 \times 256 \times 4 \approx 200$ GB — full-batch is dead
at line three, no meeting required. Probe the explosion: follow graphs
are heavy-tailed, so assume 2-hop ≈ tens of thousands; sampling is the
design, not an option. Pick by constraint: weekly retrain means epoch
time is forgiving; churn is a feature-heavy, homophily-flavored signal,
so run the SGC/SIGN candidate *first* — $\hat A^2 X$ is one sparse
multiply per week on CPU, the classifier trains in minutes, and if it
matches the sampled-SAGE candidate in the bake-off (it often will),
you have also just designed the serving story, because weekly
precomputed features plus an MLP *is* a serving architecture. Total
design time: one page of arithmetic, one afternoon of bake-off — and
every decision traceable to a measured number, which is the entire
method.

One synthesis before the pitfalls, because it is the reason this week sat
*after* the theory weeks rather than before them. Each escape is an old
friend under load: neighbor sampling is Week 7's SAGE bargain with the
variance you already measured in its widget; partitioning is Week 2's
community structure hired as a memory manager, and its bias is Week 9's
"the model can't see what isn't in the message graph" applied to the cut
edges; SGC is Week 6's spectral story taken at its word — if propagation
is a fixed low-pass filter, filter *once* — with the $K$ dial governed by
the $|\lambda_2|^K$ decay you verified numerically in HW2; GraphSAINT's
reweighting is Week 3's sampled-softmax correction; and the serving
fork's lookup table is Week 10's shallow encoder, vindicated in the one
arena it always owned. A field's scaling tricks are its theory,
compiled. If any of those correspondences surprised you, the earlier
week — not this one — is the profitable reread.

## Common pitfalls

**Comparing epochs instead of gradient steps.** One Cluster-GCN "epoch" is
40 updates in our setup; one full-batch epoch is one. Our table equalizes
*budget discipline*, not epoch counts — always check what a row calls an
epoch before reading its time column. (This is Week 7's noise-floor
lesson wearing a stopwatch.)

**Measuring peak memory with inference included.** Our first harness did —
the full-graph inference pass at the end dominated every method's peak,
reporting 1,542 MB for a sampled trainer whose true training peak was
64, and erasing the entire story of the table. Training peak and
inference peak are different budgets consumed at different times by
different hardware; report both, conflate neither, and be suspicious of
any scaling paper that does not say which one its memory column means.

**Sampling at evaluation time without averaging.** Fanout sampling at
*test* time makes predictions stochastic; production either uses full
neighborhoods for inference (our labs do), averages several samples, or
accepts the jitter knowingly. Silent test-time sampling has cost teams
weeks of "irreproducible" bug hunts.

**Trusting a random partition because our table did.** Our 0.628-on-2.5%
result is a statement about *arxiv's feature-heavy labels*, not about
partitioning. On structure-dominated tasks the same crudeness is fatal —
rerun the probe (Week 10's "measure what the graph is worth") before
borrowing the shortcut.

**Forgetting the sampler is code.** The 122× slowdown was not the model.
Profile the data pipeline first; the GPU is usually innocent and usually
idle.

**Debugging OOM by shrinking the wrong knob.** Halving the *hidden width*
halves every line of the memory bill; halving the *batch size* only
helps if memory actually scales with batch (it doesn't, for full-batch —
that is the whole point); adding layers multiplies both the explosion
and the retention. Fix OOMs with the audit in hand, not by turning dials
until the crash stops — the dial that stops the crash is often the one
that quietly killed the accuracy.

**Batch statistics that smuggle the batch.** BatchNorm inside a sampled
or clustered batch normalizes over *whatever the sampler drew* —
statistics differ between training batches, full-graph inference, and
serving one node at a time, and the mismatch surfaces as
"eval accuracy depends on batch size," one of the field's most-reported
ghost bugs. LayerNorm, or norms frozen for inference, are the standard
exorcisms.

## In this week's lab

[Lab 11](../labs/lab11.qmd) is the systems apprenticeship this lecture
kept promising: you count the explosion on arxiv yourself and match this
lecture's 18 / 4,577 / 22,663 on the same seeds; you build the CSR
structures and the fanout sampler by hand — every dedup and remap yours,
asserted for shape, bound, and determinism — and train with it; you
derive SGC on paper, implement the precompute in three sparse lines, and
beat the epoch-time column of our table on your own hardware; and you
assemble the full accuracy/time/memory comparison, with training-peak
memory measured the honest way, into a claims paragraph whose every
sentence cites cells. The closing reflection is the products
extrapolation: the arithmetic that decides, before any download, that
full-batch is impossible and which of your own implementations would
survive. (On the free Colab tier everything runs; the SGC path is
deliberately CPU-friendly, which is its entire argument.)

## Required reading

- **Hamilton, Ying, Leskovec — Inductive Representation Learning on Large
  Graphs** (NeurIPS 2017). You read it in Week 7 for the aggregators;
  reread §3 now as a systems paper — the fanout contract, the
  minibatch algorithm's bookkeeping (our Lab's sampler is its Algorithm
  2), and the inductive serving story that made the paper an industry
  document.
- **Chiang et al. — Cluster-GCN** (KDD 2019). The partition escape. §3.2's
  stochastic multi-cluster batching is the part that makes it honest;
  the memory table is the part to internalize; and note which authors'
  affiliation the paper carries — this was Google needing to train on
  graphs Google-sized.
- **Wu et al. — Simplifying Graph Convolutional Networks** (ICML 2019).
  The deletion experiment. Internalize Table 2's "same accuracy, 100×
  faster" shape, and read the abstract's tone — a null model politely
  embarrassing a subfield — as a genre you should learn to both write
  and fear.

Optional: GraphSAINT (ICLR 2020) for unbiased subgraph sampling done
right — read the estimator section as a statistics exercise; SIGN (2020)
for the multi-operator generalization and its unabashedly
production-first framing; the OGB paper (NeurIPS 2020) for why these
benchmarks exist, how their splits were designed against the leaks this
course keeps cataloguing, and what leaderboard hygiene looks like when
the graphs get big enough that nobody can afford to rerun everyone
else's baselines.

## Check your understanding

**Q1.** A 3-layer GNN, hidden width 256, on a graph of 10M nodes and 200M
edges. Estimate the float32 activation residency alone for full-batch
training, and state the verdict for a 24 GB card.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Node activations: $10^7 \times 256 \times 4$ B $\approx$ 10 GB *per layer
retained*, ×3 layers ≈ 30 GB before features, messages, gradients, or
Adam. Already over 24 GB on activations alone — full-batch is dead on
arrival; the conversation starts at sampling/partitioning, exactly as the
capacity-planning method prescribes (and as it would have told you in one
minute, before any code).
</details>

**Q2.** Our sampled SAGE ran 122× slower per epoch than full-batch while
doing less arithmetic. Reconcile, and name the two standard remedies.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
The GNN math shrank, but each batch paid a Python-loop sampler: neighbor
selection, gathers, and index remapping on CPU while the GPU waited — the
epoch is pipeline-bound, not compute-bound. Remedies: compiled parallel
samplers (pyg-lib/DGL's C++ workers) and producer-consumer overlap so
sampling for batch $k{+}1$ happens during batch $k$'s GPU work (PinSage's
MapReduce pipeline is this pattern at industrial scale).
</details>

**Q3.** Cluster-GCN with a random partition kept 2.5% of arxiv's edges yet
scored 0.628 (full-batch: 0.665). What does this measure, and why must you
not generalize it?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
It measures how much of *arxiv's* label signal lives in node features
(text embeddings) rather than in structure — with 97.5% of edges gone,
features plus a whisper of local smoothing still classify well. It is a
property of the task, not the method: on structure-dominated problems
(Week 10's typed patterns, role tasks) the between-cluster bias is
precisely the signal, and the same shortcut collapses. Probe the
graph's worth first.
</details>

**Q4.** Derive SGC from a 2-layer GCN in two lines, and name the exact
class of tasks where the derivation's deleted ingredient was load-bearing.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$\hat A\,\sigma(\hat A X W_0) W_1 \xrightarrow{\ \sigma \to \mathrm{id}\ }
\hat A^2 X (W_0 W_1) = (\hat A^2 X) W$: propagation commutes to a one-time
precompute, training is logistic regression. The deleted $\sigma$ mattered
wherever the function needs *nonlinear interactions of multi-hop
information* — heterophilous labels, combinatorial substructure signals,
Week 9's above-the-ceiling territory — anywhere "smooth then linearly
read" is not the shape of the answer.
</details>

**Q5.** Your fraud model must score a transaction against an edge created
40 seconds ago. Which serving design is forced, and what does it cost?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
On-demand inference — precomputed embeddings are stale by construction and
would miss the fresh edge entirely. The bill: a sampler plus forward pass
inside the request latency budget, GPU (or heavily optimized CPU path) in
the serving tier, and load that scales with query rate. This is why fraud
teams fund sampler engineering: the freshness requirement is the business.
</details>

**Q6.** GraphSAINT multiplies node and edge terms by inverse inclusion
probabilities. What property does this buy that Cluster-GCN lacks, and
where did this course last use the same trick?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
Unbiasedness: the expected mini-batch loss equals the full-graph loss, so
the optimizer follows the true gradient in expectation, while Cluster-GCN
systematically ignores cut edges. The same importance-correction logic
appeared in Week 3's negative sampling analysis (and Week 4's
self-adversarial weighting): reweight what you sampled by how likely you
were to sample it.
</details>

**Q7.** At fanout 10 and depth 2, give the worst-case node count per
target, and explain why depth 3 changes the sampling conversation
qualitatively.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
$1 + 10 + 100 = 111$. At depth 3 the bound is 1,111 per target — a
2,048-target batch may touch two million node-slots, rivaling the whole
graph: fanout caps tame the *base*, not the *exponent*. Hence deep
scalable GNNs pair sampling with the other escapes (precompute, or
shallow-model-deep-propagation designs), and hence production GNNs are
overwhelmingly 2–3 layers deep — which Week 9's oversmoothing was already
recommending for different reasons. Two independent walls, same door.
</details>

**Q8.** Rank our four measured methods for each scenario: (a) best
accuracy, memory no object; (b) 4 GB GPU, structure-light task, hourly
retrains; (c) 2.4M-node graph, 8 GB GPU, structure-heavy task.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>
(a) Full-batch GCN — 0.665, the table's accuracy row, and the least code.
(b) SGC — 171 MB, milliseconds per epoch, 0.638 on exactly the
feature-heavy profile it thrives on; hourly retrains are nearly free after
one precompute. (c) Sampled SAGE — partitioning's bias attacks the
structure signal you need, full-batch is ~41 GB at that scale (the stress
test's red row), so the fanout contract is what remains; budget the
pipeline engineering accordingly.
</details>

## Where this leaves us

The week's one sentence: **scaling is a negotiation between accuracy,
time, and memory, and the graph's size only ever votes on the last two.**
You measured the explosion (13% of arxiv in three hops, hubs to blame),
audited the memory bill down to the edge-message line that actually
fills the card, built the sampler and paid its 122× pipeline tax,
watched a random partition survive on 2.5% of the edges and understood
exactly why that generalizes nowhere, deleted the nonlinearity and got
0.638 from a logistic regression, and read the table like an engineer —
constraint first, then the row, then what the row costs elsewhere.

Close the loop before you leave — one minute, no notes. Reconstruct the
three escapes and the column each one sacrifices; the friendship-paradox
reason the naive $\bar d^{\,L}$ estimate was 9× too small; the serving
fork, and which side a fraud system is forced onto and why; and the one
audit you now owe every future project before its first training run.
Whichever of the four came back fuzzy is the section to reread while it
costs a minute.

Next week the *task* changes rather than the scale. Everything since Week
6 predicted properties of nodes that already exist, connected by edges we
were given. But half of graph ML's applications ask the opposite
questions: *which edges are missing* — the link prediction that Weeks 3
and 4 did with dot products and translations, now done right, with
message passing, leakage-proof splits, and a labeling trick that finally
beats the embeddings — and, stranger, *where do graphs come from at all*:
models that generate molecular graphs atom by atom, or denoise them into
existence. Prediction has been our whole world; next Thursday, the world grows a
second half — and Homework 3, released with it, will make you defend
both halves with the same measured discipline this table just taught
you.
